grades.quote: As long as the redo entries are in the log before the commitment marker, and all of them are in persistent storage before the commit operation completes, the system will ensure durability.
grades.reason: Explains write-ahead redo logging: log entries and the commit marker must reach persistent storage before commit completes, which ensures durability. It also notes that recovery reads the log and that checkpointing limits this. It is general transaction processing, not specifically filesystem crash recovery, and it gives only a partial account of replay and ignore-on-incomplete.

grades.quote: If the log is marked as containing a complete operation, then the recovery code copies the writes to where they belong in the on-disk file system. If the log is not marked as containing a complete operation, the recovery code ignores the log.
grades.reason: Directly answers the question for a filesystem. Writes are logged first, then a commit record is written, then the writes are installed, then the log is erased. On reboot, recovery replays a committed log and ignores an uncommitted one, so each operation is atomic with respect to crashes.

grades.quote: Most contemporary operating systems provide file systems that employ atomic transactions to at least maintain the structural consistency of the file system itself
grades.reason: Motivates why journaled filesystems use atomic transactions to keep metadata consistent, with examples such as rename. It does not explain how a write-ahead log enables recovery after a crash, so it is background only.
